hook.text: You partly learn from past rewards and partly from thinking about what would have worked.

buildup.text: Colin Camerer's EWA model combines reinforcement learning and belief learning into one framework.

discovery.text: EWA weights each strategy by experience: what it earned and what it would have earned if chosen.

twist.text: Newcomers lean on reinforcement. Experienced players lean on beliefs.

climax.text: EWA predicts behavior better than either learning model alone. We're neither pure trial-and-error nor pure calculators.

punchline.text: We learn from what happened and what could have happened.

quiz.question: What does the EWA model combine?

details.summary: Experience-weighted attraction is a learning model that combines belief-based and reinforcement learning, where players update the attractiveness of each strategy based on both what they actually experienced and what they would have earned from alternatives.
details.whyItMatters: EWA bridges the gap between two competing theories of how people learn in games. It provides a more accurate prediction of real behavior by capturing both the reinforcement of rewarded actions and the imagination of foregone alternatives.
takeaways: EWA combines reinforcement learning with belief-based reasoning
Players consider both received payoffs and hypothetical alternatives
The model nests simpler learning rules as special cases

faq.question: How does EWA differ from simple reinforcement learning?
faq.answer: Reinforcement learning only strengthens strategies that were played and rewarded. EWA also updates the attractiveness of strategies that were not played, based on what they would have earned. This imagined counterfactual makes learning faster.

faq.question: Is EWA practically useful outside the laboratory?
faq.answer: Yes. EWA has been applied to predict behavior in auctions, market entry games, and pricing decisions. Its flexibility in capturing different learning styles makes it useful for designing mechanisms that work well across diverse populations.
